title: Peptic Ulcer Disease and H. pylori
clientNeeds: Physiological Integrity: Reduction of Risk Potential
bottomLine: Peptic ulcer disease is commonly linked to H. pylori infection or NSAID exposure. New hematemesis, melena, sudden rigid abdominal pain, syncope, or hypotension suggests bleeding or perforation and requires emergency escalation rather than routine antacid treatment.
recognize: Epigastric burning or gnawing pain, nausea, early satiety, or occult blood loss may occur.
NSAIDs, H. pylori, smoking, prior ulcer, anticoagulation, and older age increase complication risk.
Perforation may cause sudden severe abdominal pain with guarding or rigid abdomen.
priorities: Assess pain pattern, hemodynamics, stool/emesis color, NSAID use, anticoagulants, anemia symptoms, and peritoneal signs.
Escalate active bleeding, syncope, shock, or suspected perforation.
Collect ordered H. pylori testing correctly and reinforce test-of-cure when prescribed after eradication therapy.
assessMonitor: Trend hemoglobin when bleeding is suspected, vital signs, pain, stool/emesis findings, medication adherence, and response to acid suppression/eradication therapy.
interventions: Administer proton-pump inhibitor and H. pylori eradication therapy as prescribed.
Avoid unnecessary NSAIDs and address smoking/alcohol contributors when relevant.
medicationSafety: H. pylori treatment uses multidrug regimens; incomplete therapy increases failure and resistance risk.
Bismuth can darken stool and tongue, which should not be confused automatically with GI bleeding without assessing the full clinical picture.
NSAID use with anticoagulants increases bleeding risk.
teaching: Complete the full H. pylori regimen, avoid unapproved NSAIDs, and return for recommended confirmation of eradication.
delegationScope: Routine stool observation can be delegated with clear reporting instructions; bleeding, peritoneal signs, or hemodynamic change require licensed-nurse assessment.
examTrap: Reassuring a patient with sudden rigid abdominal pain because they already have a known ulcer diagnosis.
oneLinePearl: Ulcer pain is routine until bleeding or a rigid abdomen makes it an emergency.
sourceBasis: ACG 2024 Clinical Guideline: Treatment of Helicobacter pylori Infection

title: Appendicitis: Localizing Pain and Rupture Risk
clientNeeds: Physiological Integrity: Reduction of Risk Potential
bottomLine: Appendicitis often begins with vague periumbilical pain that localizes to the right lower quadrant, with anorexia, nausea, fever, and tenderness. Sudden pain relief followed by worsening diffuse pain, rigidity, fever, or toxicity may signal perforation and peritonitis.
recognize: Pain migration toward the right lower quadrant is classic but not universal.
Children, pregnant patients, and older adults may have less typical localization.
Guarding, rebound/peritoneal irritation, persistent vomiting, or worsening fever raise concern for complicated disease.
priorities: Keep the patient NPO when surgical evaluation is likely.
Assess pain, vital signs, abdominal findings, hydration, pregnancy possibility, and progression over time.
Escalate diffuse peritoneal signs, hemodynamic instability, or rapidly worsening pain.
assessMonitor: Trend pain location/intensity, temperature, heart rate, abdominal distention/guarding, hydration, and ordered labs/imaging.
interventions: Administer prescribed IV fluids, analgesia, antiemetics, and antibiotics for complicated disease or perioperative care.
Prepare for surgical evaluation/appendectomy when indicated.
medicationSafety: Adequate analgesia should not be withheld solely to preserve the abdominal examination.
Avoid laxatives or enemas when appendicitis or bowel perforation is suspected.
redFlags: Sudden worsening after transient pain relief
teaching: Seek prompt evaluation for worsening localized abdominal pain with fever or vomiting rather than self-treating with laxatives.
delegationScope: Routine vital signs may be delegated in a stable patient; worsening abdominal findings or pain pattern requires licensed-nurse reassessment.
examTrap: Giving an enema for constipation symptoms when appendicitis is suspected.
oneLinePearl: Migrating RLQ pain suggests appendix; rigid diffuse pain suggests rupture.
sourceBasis: American College of Surgeons Appendicitis Patient and Clinical Resources

title: Bowel Obstruction: Distention, Vomiting, and Ischemia
clientNeeds: Physiological Integrity: Reduction of Risk Potential
bottomLine: Bowel obstruction causes abdominal pain/distention, vomiting, and failure to pass stool or flatus, but strangulation or ischemia is the emergency. Constant severe pain, fever, tachycardia, peritoneal signs, rising lactate, or shock requires urgent surgical escalation.
recognize: Small-bowel obstruction often causes earlier vomiting and crampy pain; distal obstruction may cause more distention.
Prior abdominal surgery raises adhesion risk; hernia, tumor, volvulus, and inflammatory disease are other causes.
High-pitched bowel sounds may occur early, but bowel sounds can become quiet later and are not sufficient to rule disease in or out.
priorities: Assess hydration, pain pattern, distention, vomiting, bowel function, hernias, peritoneal signs, and vital signs.
Keep NPO and establish ordered IV access/fluids.
Escalate constant severe pain, guarding, fever, hypotension, or suspected strangulation.
assessMonitor: Trend intake/output, NG output if used, abdominal girth when ordered, electrolytes, renal function, pain, and signs of ischemia/sepsis.
interventions: Maintain NG decompression when ordered and verify tube function according to policy.
Provide fluid/electrolyte replacement and prepare for surgery when obstruction does not resolve or ischemia/perforation is suspected.
medicationSafety: Opioids may be required but can worsen sedation and ileus; monitor effect and respiratory status.
Laxatives are inappropriate in suspected complete mechanical obstruction unless specifically directed by the treating team.
teaching: Report recurrent vomiting, inability to pass gas/stool, worsening distention, or severe constant pain promptly.
delegationScope: Routine NG output measurement may be delegated with clear parameters; tube malfunction, worsening pain, or peritoneal signs require licensed-nurse assessment.
examTrap: Giving a stimulant laxative to a patient with severe distention, vomiting, and no flatus before obstruction is excluded.
oneLinePearl: Obstruction cramps; ischemia becomes constant, toxic, and surgical.
sourceBasis: American College of Surgeons Small Bowel Obstruction Resources
World Society of Emergency Surgery Adhesive SBO Guidance

title: Inflammatory Bowel Disease: Flares, Bleeding, and Toxic Megacolon
bottomLine: Crohn disease can affect any GI segment and is transmural; ulcerative colitis involves the colon in a continuous mucosal pattern. During a severe flare, dehydration, anemia, infection, obstruction, perforation, or toxic megacolon outrank routine symptom control.
recognize: Ulcerative colitis commonly causes bloody diarrhea, urgency, and cramping.
Crohn disease more often causes abdominal pain, weight loss, diarrhea, fistulas, strictures, and perianal disease.
Fever, tachycardia, marked distention, severe tenderness, and systemic toxicity can indicate toxic megacolon in severe colitis.
priorities: Assess stool frequency/blood, hydration, weight, pain, fever, abdominal distention, nutrition, and medication adherence.
Escalate severe bleeding, obstruction, peritoneal signs, fever with marked distention, or sepsis.
Screen for infection when ordered before intensifying immunosuppression.
assessMonitor: Trend CBC, electrolytes, inflammatory markers when ordered, weight, stool pattern, hydration, and treatment adverse effects.
interventions: Administer prescribed anti-inflammatory, immunomodulator, biologic, nutritional, and supportive therapy.
Support individualized nutrition and hydration rather than imposing a single restrictive diet on all patients.
medicationSafety: Corticosteroids increase glucose, infection, and bone risks and are generally not intended as indefinite maintenance therapy.
Biologic and immunomodulator therapy requires infection screening and regimen-specific monitoring.
teaching: Do not stop maintenance therapy because symptoms improve; report fever, worsening bleeding, severe distention, or signs of infection promptly.
delegationScope: Stool counts and weights may be delegated with clear thresholds; worsening bleeding, distention, or systemic symptoms require licensed-nurse reassessment.
examTrap: Giving an antimotility drug routinely during severe colitis with marked distention and systemic toxicity.
oneLinePearl: IBD flares are common; toxic distention, sepsis, obstruction, and bleeding are the danger signals.
sourceBasis: American College of Gastroenterology Crohn Disease Guidance

title: Cholecystitis: RUQ Pain, Fever, and Obstruction Clues
clientNeeds: Physiological Integrity: Reduction of Risk Potential
bottomLine: Acute cholecystitis commonly causes persistent right upper quadrant pain, fever, nausea, and tenderness, often after gallstone obstruction. Jaundice, hypotension, confusion, or worsening cholestatic labs raise concern for common-duct obstruction or cholangitis and require urgent escalation.
recognize: Biliary colic is usually episodic after meals; cholecystitis produces more persistent inflammatory pain and tenderness.
Pain may radiate to the right shoulder or back.
Charcot-type fever, jaundice, and RUQ pain suggest ascending cholangitis; instability or confusion indicates severe disease.
priorities: Assess pain, fever, jaundice, hydration, vomiting, mental status, and sepsis signs.
Keep NPO when surgical/endoscopic evaluation is likely.
Escalate jaundice with fever, hypotension, or confusion promptly.
assessMonitor: Trend vital signs, bilirubin/liver tests when ordered, pain, hydration, and response to antibiotics/analgesia.
interventions: Administer IV fluids, analgesia, antiemetics, and antibiotics when ordered.
Prepare for laparoscopic cholecystectomy or biliary decompression based on diagnosis and severity.
medicationSafety: Opioids can cause sedation and nausea and require monitoring.
Antibiotics are guided by severity and suspected infection rather than given for uncomplicated biliary colic alone.
teaching: Seek care for fever, jaundice, or persistent RUQ pain rather than repeatedly self-treating presumed indigestion.
delegationScope: Routine comfort measures may be delegated in a stable patient; jaundice, fever, or hemodynamic change requires licensed-nurse assessment.
examTrap: Treating fever plus jaundice as routine gallbladder pain without considering ascending infection and sepsis.
oneLinePearl: RUQ pain plus fever is inflammation; add jaundice and instability and think infected obstruction.
sourceBasis: American College of Gastroenterology Biliary Disease Resources
Tokyo Guidelines Principles for Acute Cholecystitis and Cholangitis

title: Type 2 Diabetes: Protect Heart, Kidneys, Eyes, and Feet
clientNeeds: Physiological Integrity: Reduction of Risk Potential
bottomLine: Type 2 diabetes care is not only about glucose. Preventing cardiovascular, kidney, retinal, neurologic, and foot complications requires individualized glycemic goals plus blood pressure, lipid, kidney, eye, foot, smoking, nutrition, activity, and medication follow-up.
recognize: Hyperglycemia may be asymptomatic for years.
Neuropathy can reduce protective sensation and make foot injuries painless.
Albuminuria or declining eGFR can signal diabetic kidney disease before symptoms develop.
priorities: Assess glucose trends, hypoglycemia risk, medication access/adherence, foot skin and sensation, renal status, vision follow-up, cardiovascular risk, and self-management barriers.
Report infected foot wounds, rapidly rising glucose with illness, or severe hypoglycemia promptly.
assessMonitor: Follow individualized A1C/glucose targets, renal function and albuminuria, blood pressure, lipids, retinal screening, foot exams, and medication adverse effects.
interventions: Support evidence-based nutrition, physical activity, weight goals when relevant, smoking cessation, and diabetes education.
Reinforce use of medications selected for glycemic and cardiovascular/kidney benefit according to the prescribed plan.
medicationSafety: Insulin and sulfonylureas can cause hypoglycemia.
Metformin requires kidney-function review and temporary holding in selected acute illness/contrast situations per clinician direction.
SGLT2 inhibitors can increase genital infection risk and rarely contribute to ketoacidosis, sometimes with only modest glucose elevation.
teaching: Inspect feet daily, know hypoglycemia treatment, follow sick-day instructions, and keep kidney/eye/foot appointments even when glucose seems controlled.
delegationScope: Routine glucose checks may be delegated where policy permits; interpretation of symptomatic changes or foot deterioration requires licensed-nurse assessment.
examTrap: Focusing only on A1C while ignoring kidney decline, foot injury, blood pressure, or cardiovascular risk.
oneLinePearl: Diabetes care protects organs, not just numbers.
sourceBasis: American Diabetes Association Standards of Care in Diabetes—2026

title: Hyperosmolar Hyperglycemic State: Extreme Dehydration
bottomLine: HHS is severe hyperglycemia with hyperosmolality and profound dehydration, usually with little or no significant ketoacidosis. Neurologic change, hypotension, and extreme volume deficit are major threats; treatment requires careful fluids, insulin, electrolyte monitoring, and correction of the precipitating illness.
recognize: HHS often develops over days to weeks with polyuria, polydipsia, progressive dehydration, weakness, and altered mental status.
It is more common in older adults with type 2 diabetes and is often triggered by infection, missed therapy, stroke, MI, or medications.
DKA and HHS can overlap, so laboratory assessment guides treatment.
priorities: Assess ABCs, mental status, perfusion, hydration, glucose, electrolytes, osmolality, and precipitating illness.
Begin ordered IV fluid resuscitation and monitor closely for heart/kidney limitations.
Administer insulin and electrolyte replacement according to the hyperglycemic-crisis protocol.
assessMonitor: Trend glucose, sodium, potassium, osmolality, renal function, urine output, hemodynamics, and neurologic status.
Monitor for thrombosis, fluid overload, hypoglycemia, and overly rapid osmotic shifts.
interventions: Use gradual correction targets because overly rapid changes in osmolality can cause neurologic injury.
medicationSafety: Insulin lowers potassium, so potassium must be monitored and corrected as needed.
Older adults with heart or kidney disease require careful fluid administration.
Do not stop therapy just because the glucose has fallen if hyperosmolality and clinical dehydration persist.
teaching: Follow sick-day glucose monitoring and hydration plans and seek care early for persistent hyperglycemia, dehydration, or inability to take fluids.
delegationScope: HHS is unstable; frequent measurements may be delegated only within protocol while the PN/RN team continuously evaluates trends and deterioration.
examTrap: Assuming HHS is resolved as soon as glucose falls below the initial extreme level.
oneLinePearl: HHS is a hyperosmolar dehydration emergency—fix the patient, not just the glucose.
sourceBasis: American Diabetes Association Standards of Care in Diabetes—2026

title: Hypothyroidism: Slow Metabolism, Safe Replacement
bottomLine: Hypothyroidism causes metabolic slowing: fatigue, cold intolerance, constipation, dry skin, slowed heart rate, depression/cognitive changes, and weight gain can occur. Levothyroxine replacement is effective but requires consistent administration and TSH-based follow-up; severe decompensation is a different emergency addressed as myxedema coma.
recognize: Symptoms are nonspecific, so diagnosis relies on thyroid testing rather than symptoms alone.
Older adults may present subtly with fatigue, cognitive decline, or bradycardia.
Pregnancy changes thyroid-hormone requirements and needs prompt clinician follow-up.
priorities: Assess symptoms, heart rate, bowel pattern, medication timing/adherence, pregnancy status, and factors that interfere with levothyroxine absorption.
Report marked bradycardia, severe hypothermia, or progressive altered mental status as possible decompensation.
assessMonitor: Trend TSH and free T4 as ordered after medication changes and during special situations such as pregnancy.
Monitor for over-replacement symptoms including palpitations, tremor, heat intolerance, or insomnia.
interventions: Administer levothyroxine consistently at the same time and under consistent fasting/food conditions according to the prescribed plan.
Separate interacting supplements/medications such as calcium and iron according to pharmacist/provider guidance.
medicationSafety: Too much thyroid hormone can trigger tachyarrhythmias and bone loss over time.
Do not stop levothyroxine abruptly without clinician guidance.
Biotin can interfere with some thyroid laboratory tests and should be disclosed before testing.
teaching: Take thyroid hormone consistently, disclose calcium/iron/biotin and other medications, and arrange prompt thyroid review when pregnancy is planned or confirmed.
delegationScope: Routine medication administration may fall within PN scope; interpretation of thyroid dose changes remains provider-directed.
examTrap: Taking levothyroxine together with calcium and iron supplements every morning without considering absorption interference.
oneLinePearl: Thyroid replacement works best when the dose and the way it is taken stay consistent.
sourceBasis: American Thyroid Association Hypothyroidism and Thyroid Hormone Treatment Resources
American Thyroid Association 2026 Pregnancy/Postpartum Thyroid Guideline where applicable

title: Hyperthyroidism: Heat, Heart Rate, and Antithyroid Safety
clientNeeds: Physiological Integrity: Reduction of Risk Potential
bottomLine: Hyperthyroidism causes metabolic acceleration: heat intolerance, weight loss, tremor, anxiety, tachycardia, diarrhea, and muscle weakness are common. Monitor rhythm and weight, give prescribed antithyroid/beta-blocking therapy safely, and recognize fever, delirium, heart failure, or extreme tachycardia as possible thyroid storm.
recognize: Graves disease may include goiter and eye findings.
Older adults may present with atrial fibrillation, weight loss, or weakness rather than obvious tremor and anxiety.
Low TSH with elevated thyroid hormones supports overt hyperthyroidism but etiology determines definitive treatment.
priorities: Assess heart rate/rhythm, weight, temperature tolerance, bowel pattern, sleep, tremor, and eye symptoms.
Report new atrial fibrillation, severe tachycardia, fever, delirium, or heart-failure signs immediately.
assessMonitor: Trend thyroid tests, heart rate, weight, and treatment adverse effects.
Monitor CBC/liver-related symptoms when antithyroid medications are used according to the prescribed plan.
interventions: Administer beta blockers for symptom control and antithyroid medication as ordered.
Provide eye comfort measures for Graves orbitopathy and reinforce smoking cessation because smoking worsens thyroid eye disease.
medicationSafety: Methimazole is usually preferred for many nonpregnant patients, but pregnancy can alter drug selection and requires specialist guidance.
Fever or sore throat while taking an antithyroid drug can signal agranulocytosis and requires prompt evaluation.
Jaundice or severe abdominal symptoms can signal hepatotoxicity and need urgent review.
teaching: Report fever/sore throat immediately while taking antithyroid drugs, keep thyroid-lab follow-up, and do not stop therapy without guidance.
delegationScope: Routine vital signs may be delegated in stable patients; new tachyarrhythmia, fever, or neurologic change requires licensed-nurse assessment.
examTrap: Reassuring a patient on methimazole who reports fever and sore throat without arranging urgent blood-count evaluation.
oneLinePearl: Hyperthyroid patients run hot and fast; fever plus sore throat on antithyroid drugs is not routine.
sourceBasis: American Thyroid Association Hyperthyroidism and Thyrotoxicosis Guidance
American Thyroid Association 2026 Pregnancy/Postpartum Thyroid Guideline where applicable
